A deadlock is when two or more threads (or processes) are each waiting for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed. The classic case: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.

It requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion (a resource can be held by only one thread), hold-and-wait (a thread keeps what it has while waiting for more), no preemption (resources can't be forcibly taken away), and circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting on the next). Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

The most practical fix is to break circular wait by always acquiring locks in the same global order everywhere in the code. If every thread takes lock 1 before lock 2, the cycle can't form.

When ordering isn't feasible, use a try-lock with a timeout and release everything you hold on failure, then retry with backoff; this breaks hold-and-wait. Beyond that, reduce the opportunity: hold locks for as short a time as possible, never call unknown code (callbacks, I/O) while holding one, and prefer a single coarse lock, immutable data, or message passing over many fine-grained locks.

Databases take the remaining approach, detection and recovery: they find the wait cycle and abort one transaction, so your code should be ready to retry a transaction that fails as a deadlock victim.
